title: My Daily Brief
overview: US midterm results dominate this edition. Democrats flipped a North Carolina Senate seat and a western North Carolina House seat, and held Senate seats in Georgia and New Hampshire, while Republican Byron Donalds won Florida's governorship. Abroad, Binance published its account of a $6 billion-plus crypto theft the FBI blames on North Korea, Pyongyang fired another projectile, and Canva announced a restructuring affecting 22% of its staff.

stories.headline: Roy Cooper wins North Carolina Senate race, flipping a Republican-held seat
stories.summary: Former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper defeated Republican Michael Whatley, a former RNC chair recruited by President Trump, for the seat being vacated by retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis. Outlets described it as Democrats' first Senate flip of the night and a step toward their goal of retaking the chamber. Cooper focused his campaign on cost of living and health care and promised to be an "independent" senator. Major outside groups on both sides had pulled back spending weeks earlier as Cooper's polling lead held. Democrats still need to net more Republican-held seats to win a majority.
key_facts: The AP called the race for Cooper at about 8:23 p.m. ET on Nov. 3.
Early returns showed Cooper with roughly 66% to Whatley's 32%, with a little over half the vote counted.
It was Cooper's seventh straight statewide win. North Carolina had not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008.
Republicans entered the election with a 53-seat Senate majority.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian placed the win within a broader Democratic push for the Senate, which it linked to Trump's unpopularity over the economy, Iran and immigration. It stressed what Senate control would let Democrats do: block bills, issue subpoenas and reject judicial nominees. PBS/AP focused on the victory party and quoted Cooper on tariffs and the cost of fuel and fertilizer "because of this never-ending war." It also quoted Gov. Josh Stein calling the result "competence over chaos."
Axios and Queen City News gave straightforward results coverage. Axios emphasized Cooper's popularity, his name recognition and the fact that he has never lost an election.

Fox News and the Washington Examiner covered the race as a clear Democratic win. They noted that GOP groups had pulled out early and that Trump appeared at a rally to concede Cooper would likely win. The Examiner quoted Tillis saying Whatley's "patently partisan resume" hurt him in a year it called a rebuke of Trump. It also noted that Republicans had tried to tie Cooper's tenure to rising crime. Fox covered Lara Trump's decision not to run.

disputed: Partial vote shares differ slightly between Fox (66.4% to 32.0%) and the Washington Examiner (66.8% to 31.6%); final margins were not yet reported.
Whether the result reflects a broader national rebuke of Trump is an interpretation offered by some outlets and by Tillis, not a settled fact.
stories.why: The flip narrows the path Republicans need to keep control of the Senate for the last two years of Trump's term.

stories.headline: Binance says fake job interviews and an internal AI tool enabled record crypto theft
stories.summary: Binance published a postmortem on last week's theft of more than $6 billion, which the FBI attributes to a North Korean hacking group it calls TraderTraitor. According to Binance, the multi-stage campaign began in June, when an engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installer. In September, a second engineer was hit through fake recruitment interviews that ended with a malware-laden "assignment." On Oct. 20, the attackers used an internal AI tool to reach credentials, and on Oct. 29 they launched unauthorized transactions through the company's wallet signing service. Executive Richard Teng said Binance is absorbing the full loss and that 98% of affected assets have been replenished. North Korea has rejected the FBI's attribution.
key_facts: The breach began in June 2026, and the theft was executed on Oct. 29 between 17:15 and 19:56.
Binance says about $2.85 billion in stolen assets has been frozen or intercepted.
Binance says it blocked 57 suspected North Korea-linked threats.
Teng said customers lost nothing: "The full financial impact will be borne by us."
The FBI says the hackers converted stolen assets mainly into Ether.

perspectives.framing: The Verge laid out the attack timeline, then questioned why such a well-known tactic worked. It noted that warnings about job-interview code downloads have circulated for years, and that Binance gave little detail on the internal AI tool or why it helped the attackers.

The Hacker News, Axios, The Hill and the Korea Herald focused on technical details and the job-market angle. Axios framed it as North Korea "weaponizing both sides of the job market." The Korea Herald added Kim Yo-jong's rejection of the FBI's findings and a State Department comment calling DPRK cybercrime a global problem.

Fox Business centered on Teng's interview and reassurances that customers won't "lose a dime." It emphasized Binance's reserves and its SAFU fund, and Teng's statement that flows have returned to normal.

disputed: The reported amount varies: $6.43 billion (The Hacker News), $6.34 billion (Korea Herald) and $6.3 billion (several others).
North Korea denies involvement and calls the FBI attribution a provocation.
Little is known about the internal AI tool and how it was exploited.
Binance's statements about full reimbursement and normalized flows are the company's own claims.
stories.why: The heist shows how state-backed hackers combine social engineering with companies' own AI tools, a risk that extends well beyond crypto.

stories.headline: Jon Ossoff wins re-election in Georgia over Rep. Mike Collins
stories.summary: Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff defeated Republican Rep. Mike Collins in Georgia, a state Trump won in 2024. Ossoff campaigned on affordability and attacked Collins over his support for Trump's tariffs and the war in Iran. Collins emphasized immigration, including the Laken Riley Act he authored. Republican groups pulled back spending in mid-October, and the race was called less than an hour after polls closed. The result is likely to fuel speculation about a 2028 presidential run, which Ossoff has said he has no interest in.
key_facts: Collins won a June GOP runoff with a late Trump endorsement, defeating Kemp-backed Derek Dooley.
Ossoff was the only Senate Democrat defending a seat in a state Trump carried in 2024.
Ossoff has said he has "zero interest" in running for president in 2028.

perspectives.framing: NPR stressed Collins's "personal baggage": ties to family members and former staffers who espoused white nationalist and antisemitic views, and his embrace of Trump's false 2020 fraud claims. It contrasted this with Ossoff's constituent services and national appeal. PBS/AP noted Ossoff's fundraising dominance and the GOP spending pullback.
The BBC highlighted Ossoff as a Democratic "rising star" and his 2028 prospects. It covered his cost-of-living message and noted that Gov. Kemp declined to run. The Hill provided brief results.

Fox News framed it as a GOP failure to flip a prized seat. It presented both campaigns' arguments, including Collins's immigration focus and inflation attacks, and mentioned the House ethics probe and his son-in-law's posts. The Washington Examiner gave brief results.

disputed: Collins describes the House ethics matter as a meritless "complaint."
Early vote shares (about 80% to 20% with 11% reporting, per The Hill) are not indicative of the final margin.
stories.why: Holding Georgia is a precondition for any Democratic Senate majority and raises Ossoff's national profile.

stories.headline: Democrat Jamie Ager flips North Carolina's 11th District House seat
stories.summary: Democrat Jamie Ager, a farmer and business owner, defeated Republican state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom in western North Carolina's 11th District, a seat Trump carried by 11 points in 2024. Balkcom replaced Rep. Chuck Edwards on the ballot after he ended his campaign; Edwards was later censured by the House over inappropriate conduct toward female staffers. Recovery from Hurricane Helene was a central issue. Other North Carolina House races were still being counted when reports were filed.
key_facts: The AP called the race at 8:53 p.m., with Ager at 60.3% to Balkcom's 38.4% and 83% counted.
In the third quarter, Ager raised $2.3 million to Balkcom's $355,134.
Ager's grandfather, James McClure Clarke, represented the district nearly 40 years ago.
Rep. Alma Adams easily won re-election in the 12th District.

perspectives.framing: WFAE placed the flip in a roundup of tight Charlotte-area races where Republican incumbents were trailing in early counts. It emphasized GOP redistricting that had already shifted the state delegation to 10-4. PBS/AP stressed Ager's farming background and appeal to rural voters.
Queen City News focused on the celebration at Ager's watch party. The Hill noted Edwards's censure as the reason the seat was open.

The Washington Examiner covered the Edwards scandal and Balkcom's short window to campaign. It highlighted Helene recovery, including Vice President Vance's announcement of nearly $900 million in aid, and noted Ager's fundraising advantage.

disputed: Several other North Carolina House races (the 1st, 8th, 9th, 10th and 14th districts) were undecided at the time of reporting.
stories.why: This was described as Democrats' first House pickup of the night, in a district Trump won comfortably.

stories.headline: Byron Donalds elected Florida governor, the state's first Black governor
stories.summary: Republican Rep. Byron Donalds defeated Democrat David Jolly, a former Republican congressman, to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis. The AP called the race at 9:09 p.m., with Donalds at about 50% to Jolly's 48.7%. That margin was narrow for a state Trump won by 13 points. Affordability, property insurance and AI data centers were central issues. Donalds, who is backed by Trump, briefly removed Trump references from his website in September but rallied with the president late in the race.
key_facts: The AP called the race at 9:09 p.m. ET, with Donalds at about 50% and Jolly at 48.7%.
No Democrat has won Florida's governorship since 1994.
By August, Donalds had raised more than $100 million to Jolly's roughly $10 million.
Florida has about 1.5 million more registered Republicans than Democrats.

perspectives.framing: NPR and The Guardian noted Trump's backing and the national backdrop of discontent over gas prices and the Iran war. The Guardian emphasized DeSantis's culture-war record, Democratic heavyweights campaigning for Jolly, and the challenges the new governor inherits. NPR mentioned Jolly's "data center Donalds" attack.

Newsweek emphasized the historic stakes for both candidates, the polling, and the issue debates over data centers and insurance. It noted that Donalds's proximity to Trump was a difficult issue for him. The Hill gave brief results.

Fox News highlighted the historic win, calling Donalds the first Black Republican elected governor in US history. It quoted his victory statement and his attacks on Jolly's "radical socialism." The Washington Examiner emphasized his outreach to Black voters and his fundraising edge.

disputed: Jolly called Donalds a "liar" over the socialism charges, saying he has condemned socialism many times.
Reported vote shares differ slightly (50.1% vs. 50%), and final results were not yet available.
stories.why: Florida's next governor will shape policy in the third-most-populous state, and the narrow margin may signal shifting GOP strength.

stories.headline: Chris Pappas wins New Hampshire Senate seat, keeping it in Democratic hands
stories.summary: Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas defeated former Republican Sen. John Sununu for the seat held by retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. He becomes the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. Sununu conceded early, with about 20% of the vote counted. Republicans had considered the state a top pickup target. In his speech, Pappas attacked corporate interests, Trump and "cowards in Congress," and pledged to oppose data centers and ICE detention facilities.
key_facts: Pappas led about 61% to 38% with roughly 20% of the vote counted.
Sununu was endorsed by Trump but distanced himself from the president.
Pappas will take office in January.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian emphasized the historic milestone and Pappas's populist victory speech, quoting it at length. It portrayed Sununu as a candidate Pappas cast as a "faux moderate," and noted that Sununu said he had "never met" Trump.
The BBC, Axios and The Hill covered it as a must-hold for Democrats and a missed GOP opportunity. They noted Sununu's political dynasty and Thune's campaigning for him.

Fox News presented both candidates' arguments in their own words. It quoted Sununu calling Pappas an underachiever and a "rubber stamp for the far left," and Pappas citing his bipartisan record and his challenge to Biden on the border.

disputed: Pappas's claim that "outright lies" were used against him and Sununu's characterizations of Pappas are campaign assertions.
stories.why: Holding New Hampshire was considered essential to any Democratic path to a Senate majority.

stories.headline: North Korea fires unidentified projectile toward the sea, South Korea says
stories.summary: South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said North Korea fired an unidentified projectile off its east coast on Wednesday, without giving details. The launch follows a barrage of about a dozen short-range ballistic missiles last Thursday and recent cluster-munition tests. Kim Yo Jong issued a new statement rejecting dialogue with the US after the FBI blamed Pyongyang for the Binance heist. Inter-Korean tensions have also risen since mine blasts at the border in September wounded three South Korean soldiers.
key_facts: The launch occurred Wednesday, Nov. 4, local time, according to the JCS.
North Korea fired around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles from the Wonsan area last Thursday.
Kim Yo Jong said: "we have no need to sit face to face with such unreliable and hostile persons."

perspectives.framing: PBS/AP gave broader context. It suggested the tests are likely aimed at gaining leverage in potential diplomacy with Trump, and linked the launch to the Binance dispute and border tensions.
Yonhap and the Korea Herald gave brief, factual reports. They noted the launch came less than a week after Seoul proposed military talks.

disputed: The type of weapon has not been disclosed.

Accounts of the cluster-munition tests differ: Yonhap says a cluster bomb for tactical ballistic missiles was tested Saturday, while AP cites a cluster warhead for strategic cruise missiles tested Monday. These may be separate tests.
North Korea denies planting the border mines.
stories.why: The escalating tests and Pyongyang's rejection of talks complicate any US-North Korea diplomacy.

stories.headline: Canva restructuring to affect 1,271 jobs, 22% of its workforce
stories.summary: Canva CEO Melanie Perkins announced that 1,271 employees will be laid off, relocated or moved to new roles, calling it "the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history." The company is merging teams, making Sydney the primary home for more product teams, and requiring most hybrid workers to spend two to three days in the office starting in January. Departing staff will receive at least six months' salary and extended healthcare. The exact number of job losses was not specified.
key_facts: 1,271 people, or 22% of staff, are affected.
Perkins said growth slowed for the first time in a decade.
Backers reportedly cut Canva's valuation from A$60bn to about A$49bn.
Departing staff can apply for US$10,000 grants to start their own ventures.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian placed the cuts in a wave of tech restructurings (Atlassian, Block, WiseTech) and the "SaaS-pocalypse" debate, while noting that Canva itself did not mention AI. The Verge quoted Perkins on "refounding" Canva and noted Squarespace's layoffs.
The BBC linked the move to reported valuation drops tied to concerns about AI's impact on Canva's business and the cost of building AI products.

disputed: The role of AI is unclear: the BBC cites AI-related concerns and costs, while The Guardian notes the announcement did not mention AI.
How many of the 1,271 will lose their jobs, rather than relocate or change roles, has not been disclosed.
stories.why: It is another sign of pressure on established software companies as AI reshapes the industry.

stories.headline: Korean weather agency chief explains how a Nankai Trough quake could affect South Korea
stories.summary: In a Korea Herald op-ed, Korea Meteorological Administration head Lee Mi-seon explained how long-period ground motion from a major Japanese earthquake could make high-rise buildings in South Korea sway through resonance. She cited Japan's estimate that a maximum-class Nankai Trough quake could kill about 298,000 people. She also pointed to past cases where distant quakes shook tall buildings in Osaka and Bangkok. This is an opinion and explainer piece, not breaking news.
key_facts: Japan estimates a maximum-class Nankai Trough quake could kill about 298,000 people and destroy about 2.35 million buildings.
A magnitude 7.1 quake in Kumamoto on July 28 prompted 789 shaking reports in Korea.

perspectives.framing: The only coverage is an official's explanatory op-ed focused on public safety and building response.

stories.why: Residents of tall buildings in South Korea may face risks from earthquakes hundreds of kilometers away.

stories.headline: Senior North Korean party official visits China
stories.summary: Kim Song-nam, a Workers' Party politburo member and party secretary, arrived in China on Tuesday leading a delegation at the invitation of the Chinese Communist Party, according to North Korean state media. The trip comes 10 days after Kim Jong-un made a surprise visit to the border city of Dandong. Yonhap describes it as part of warming ties after a chill over Pyongyang's closeness to Russia. A Chinese party school delegation is visiting Pyongyang at the same time.
key_facts: Kim Song-nam's delegation was greeted by Sun Haiyan of the CCP's International Liaison Department.
Xie Chuntao of the CCP Central Party School arrived in Pyongyang on Monday.

perspectives.framing: Yonhap reported the visit based on KCNA and framed it as evidence of deepening North Korea–China cooperation.

disputed: The agenda for the visit has not been disclosed.
stories.why: Closer Beijing-Pyongyang ties could affect diplomacy over North Korea's weapons programs.

investigations.question: What is happening with AI regulation in the US and EU?
investigations.update: The Guardian reports that US tech stocks recovered on Tuesday after a selloff driven by worries about AI spending. It says investors expect Democrats to win the House and possibly gain Senate seats, which could lead to more AI regulation. This is an expectation, not policy action. Nothing in this edition addresses EU AI regulation.
